ChannelTokenFormer's channel-summary tokens, variable token counts, structured attention, and patch masking form a coherent architecture for heterogeneous-length inputs.

The evaluation has useful breadth: three modified benchmarks, one industrial dataset, multiple horizons and missingness ratios, five-seed error bars, conventional-setting results, and several component and attention-mask ablations.
The presentation is generally clear, with helpful architecture diagrams, detailed result tables, and qualitative forecasts.
weaknesses: The missingness comparison is substantially unfair: CTF is explicitly trained with random patch masking and receives missingness masks, whereas the baselines are apparently trained normally and merely receive zero-filled missing blocks at test time. Missing-aware or irregular-time methods discussed in the related work, such as SERT, BRITS, GRU-D, RAINDROP, and recent irregular forecasting models, are not evaluated.

The proposed asynchronous setting is narrow and mostly synthetic. Channels are deterministically downsampled from aligned regular benchmarks, so the experiments do not test phase offsets, non-integer sampling ratios, sampling jitter, or genuine irregular timestamps. The main missingness experiment is limited to SolarWind and constructs blocks to span exactly one model patch, directly favoring the proposed masking mechanism.

Important algorithmic details are underspecified: the threshold defining a 'strong' FFT frequency, the fallback patch rule, treatment of remainder and partially missing patches, FFT computation under missingness, handling of unseen patch lengths, positional encoding in physical time, and decoder construction for heterogeneous horizons are unclear. This prevents reliable reproduction and leaves edge cases unresolved.

The spectral justification contains technical errors. A centered triangular interpolation kernel has a real sinc-squared response and does not produce the claimed frequency-dependent negative phase delay. The discussion of interpolation creating beyond-Nyquist energy and the universal energy inequality is also misleading without carefully accounting for upsampling images, normalization, and the unavailable continuous-time ground truth.

The comparison confounds architecture with supervision and preprocessing: baselines are trained on interpolated grids and apparently optimize losses involving synthesized values, while CTF excludes such indices. Evaluating on shared observed targets does not remove this training-objective disadvantage. Mask-aware adaptations and equalized training augmentations are needed.

Reproducibility is limited: there is no code or public practical-dataset release, the proprietary CHS dataset lacks sample counts, splits, detailed channel selection, and access information, and several core hyperparameters and preprocessing choices are missing.

The gains without missingness are generally modest, while parameter count, runtime, memory, and scaling experiments are absent despite efficiency claims and acknowledged quadratic attention. Overall, the central empirical claims are not sufficiently isolated or supported for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: Addresses a practically important combination of multivariate forecasting challenges: heterogeneous channel sampling rates, cross-channel dependence, and block-wise test-time missingness.
The channel-token architecture is coherent and reasonably intuitive, combining variable-length channel representations, structured attention, and patch masking in a unified model.
The paper compares against several forecasting architectures, reports five-seed error bars for its principal settings, and includes component and attention-mask ablations.
The manuscript is generally clear and visually polished, and it acknowledges scalability and long-horizon smoothing limitations.
weaknesses: The central evaluation is substantially confounded. Baselines are trained on interpolated targets with ordinary MSE and receive zero-filled missing blocks without masks, whereas CTF is trained only on native observations, receives explicit missingness information, and uses 40% random patch masking. The paper even describes this setup as amplifying differences. Consequently, the results do not establish that the proposed architecture is better under otherwise comparable conditions. Missing-aware or irregular-time baselines, masked-loss adaptations, and equivalent missingness augmentation are needed.

Most evidence for asynchrony comes from synthetically downsampled versions of standard datasets using manually assigned sampling rates. Block-wise missingness is evaluated primarily on only one constructed SolarWind dataset, with blocks tailored to the proposed patch mechanism. The real industrial dataset does not validate the missingness claim and is insufficiently documented for independent scrutiny.

The method does not explicitly model observation timestamps or temporal offsets across channels. Cross-channel interaction occurs through globally summarized channel tokens, so it is unclear how temporally aligned lagged relationships are represented. The treatment of variable sequence lengths alone does not fully support the broad claim of modeling asynchronous observations.

The frequency-based patching procedure is underspecified: the criterion for a 'strong' dominant frequency, handling of the DC component, fallback rule, FFT computation when inputs contain missing values, rounding and boundary behavior, and decoder details are not adequately defined. This limits reproducibility and makes the corresponding ablation difficult to interpret.

The interpolation analysis contains technical errors. Multiplication by a sinc-squared response cannot create spectral support where the input spectrum is zero, and an ideal centered triangular kernel has no frequency-dependent phase delay; a shifted implementation produces linear phase. The asserted universal energy inequality is also not justified. These issues undermine the paper's theoretical explanation, while the empirical spectral differences are very small and lack uncertainty estimates.

The architectural novelty is limited: learned summary tokens, structured attention masks, frequency-informed patching, and patch dropout are established ideas, and the paper mainly combines them for this setting. The empirical design is not rigorous enough to demonstrate that this combination constitutes a strong top-tier contribution.

Important reproducibility and efficiency information is missing, including code or data availability, dataset splits and sample counts, normalization details, selection criteria for the 10 proprietary CHS channels, complete per-model tuning, parameter counts, runtime, and memory usage. This is especially problematic because the paper itself identifies quadratic channel scaling as a limitation.

Several reported gains in the asynchronous setting are modest, yet the main tables aggregate across horizons and do not provide statistical tests. The conventional forecasting results are mixed rather than consistently state of the art, further weakening claims of broad superiority.

strengths: The paper targets an important and practically motivated combination of multivariate forecasting challenges: channel dependencies, heterogeneous sampling periods, and block-wise test-time missingness.

ChannelTokenFormer is a coherent design: channel tokens provide fixed-size channel summaries, structured attention separates local temporal modeling from cross-channel communication, and patch masking supports variable observed-token counts.

The empirical study is broad, covering three modified benchmarks, one industrial dataset, multiple forecasting horizons, seven representative baselines, conventional regularly sampled benchmarks, and five-seed error bars.

The results are consistently favorable in the proposed settings, with especially clear robustness gains as the missing ratio increases. Component and attention-mask ablations generally support the architectural choices.
The presentation is clear and well organized, with useful diagrams, detailed supplementary tables, and an explicit discussion of scalability and long-horizon smoothing limitations.
weaknesses: The missingness comparison is materially confounded: CTF is trained with random patch masking tuned to the test corruption, whereas the baselines appear to be trained on complete inputs and only exposed to zero-filled blocks at test time. Training baselines with the same block-corruption augmentation, or comparing against missing-aware forecasting and imputation methods, is necessary to substantiate the central robustness claim.

The missing-block construction is tailored to the proposed mechanism: SolarWind blocks span exactly one patch, ensuring they can be removed perfectly. Handling of partially missing patches is unclear, even though this is the more general case and the point-level mask in the formulation suggests it should be supported.

The asynchronous benchmarks are largely synthetic multirate resamplings with fixed periods, rather than genuinely asynchronous observations with differing offsets or irregular acquisition times. No direct comparisons are made to the irregular-time models discussed in related work, limiting the scope of the claimed real-world generality.

Several essential method details are underspecified, including the threshold defining a strong FFT peak, the fallback patch-length rule, whether patch lengths are determined per sample or globally, management of projection layers for changing patch lengths, and the decoder used for heterogeneous horizons.

The spectral argument contains technical problems. Under the paper's own equation, multiplication by a sinc-squared response cannot create energy where the input spectrum is zero, and a real nonnegative sinc-squared response does not produce the claimed frequency-dependent phase delay. The spectral experiment is also narrow and shows only very small improvements without uncertainty estimates.

Reproducibility is incomplete: dataset sizes and splits, preprocessing details, full optimization settings, and code availability are not clearly specified. The proprietary CHS dataset and the selection of 10 out of 52 channels are insufficiently documented for independent validation.

The practical-setting gains are sometimes modest, and comparisons combine different input representations and channel-specific decoders. Together with the evaluation confounds, the evidence falls slightly short of supporting acceptance at a top-tier venue despite the paper's promising idea and extensive experiments.

strengths: Addresses a practically important combination of heterogeneous channel sampling, cross-channel dependence, and test-time missing intervals within one forecasting framework.
The channel-token architecture is clearly presented and provides a sensible way to summarize variable numbers of channel-specific patches.
Evaluation covers several architectures, six practical-setting datasets, multiple horizons, five-seed error bars, ablations, scalability measurements, and conventional forecasting benchmarks.
The reported results are generally strong in the proposed asynchronous setting, including consistent gains on ETT1, SolarWind, Weather, EPA, and CHS.
The paper is well organized, includes an ethics discussion, and provides useful implementation and dataset details.
weaknesses: The contribution is primarily an integration of established ingredients—channel summary tokens, frequency-guided patching, patch dropout, and structured attention masks—so the methodological novelty is limited.

The dynamic-patching definition appears technically inconsistent. The dominant period is computed from an already downsampled channel as p*=Li/k*, but the patch length then divides it by the sampling factor again. In the SolarWind example, a 72-sample solar period is reduced to 18 samples, which no longer represents the detected period. Moreover, the maximum spectral amplitude will almost always exceed its own 70th percentile, making the stated fallback criterion effectively vacuous.

The missingness comparison is substantially confounded: CTF is explicitly trained with 40% patch masking, while most competing forecasters do not appear to receive comparable missingness augmentation. SolarWind missing blocks are also constructed to span exactly one CTF patch, directly matching its removal mechanism. This weakens the central robustness claim.

Most practical datasets are artificially downsampled versions of synchronized benchmarks with fixed, commensurate periods, rather than naturally asynchronous or irregular observations. The complete missingness comparison is largely restricted to SolarWind; the EPA extension uses only two baselines, excludes BiTGraph after convergence failure, and does not consistently favor CTF in CMSE.

Baseline fidelity is questionable: several methods are reimplemented, and ContiFormer's ODE solver is replaced with an approximation based on a different architecture. Without validation against official implementations, these results do not establish fair state-of-the-art comparisons.

The spectral analysis contains questionable claims. A triangular linear-interpolation kernel has a sinc-squared magnitude response and does not by itself imply the asserted frequency-dependent phase delay; the discussion of interpolation introducing beyond-Nyquist energy is also insufficiently specified. The empirical spectral differences in Table 6 are very small and lack uncertainty or significance analysis.

The method removes only fully missing patches, leaving unclear how partially missing patches are represented. This is especially important for the short 5–20-step missing blocks used in ETT1 and EPA, which need not align with patch boundaries.

Reproducibility claims are internally inconsistent: the appendix reports five random seeds, while the reproducibility statement says three. It also claims that software versions and private-data split statistics are provided, but these are not actually specified, and code is deferred until publication.

Several explanatory conclusions are speculative—for example, attributing the optimal number of channel tokens to particular latent channel groups—without quantitative clustering or attention evidence. Parameter counts and controlled efficiency comparisons are also missing.

strengths: The paper targets a practically important combination of multirate sampling, cross-channel dependence, and test-time missing blocks that is often studied only in isolation.

ChannelTokenFormer is conceptually coherent: channel tokens provide fixed-size summaries, structured attention separates local and cross-channel interactions, and patch masking permits variable observed-token counts.

The empirical study covers several architectures, multiple forecasting horizons, conventional and proposed settings, ablations, five-seed error bars, and basic scalability measurements. The reported results are generally favorable, particularly on EPA and under severe SolarWind missingness.
The paper is readable, well organized, and includes limitations and an ethics statement.
weaknesses: The evaluation setting is largely synthetic and favors the proposed inductive biases. Four benchmark datasets are manually downsampled using ad hoc domain-motivated rates, while the principal block-missing experiment uses blocks aligned exactly to CTF's patch lengths. This does not establish robustness to naturally occurring asynchronous observations or arbitrary missing intervals.

Baseline fairness is inadequate. Regular baselines are forced through interpolation, whereas CTF receives masks and native observations; only TimeXer receives a modified interpolation-free variant, and that variant beats CTF on ETT2. Other strong baselines are not comparably adapted. ContiFormer is replaced by an unspecified approximation of its ODE solver, so its result cannot reliably represent the published method.

The central frequency-domain justification contains questionable or incorrect claims. A centered triangular interpolation kernel has a real sinc-squared response and does not inherently produce the asserted frequency-dependent negative phase delay. The discussion also conflates continuous reconstruction, discrete resampling, spectral images, and leakage. Table 6 shows extremely small differences and only one example, so it does not substantiate the strong claim that interpolation distortion explains forecasting gains.

Important method details are ambiguous. It is unclear whether FFT periods are estimated per window, channel, or training set; the fallback patching rule is not specified; the 70th-percentile peak test appears potentially vacuous; and dividing an FFT period measured on an already subsampled channel by the sampling factor may double-correct for resolution. The decoder and handling of partially observed patches are also insufficiently formalized.

Cross-channel timing is not convincingly modeled. Local positional embeddings index samples rather than physical timestamps, so equal indices across channels can denote different times. Compressing each channel into global tokens may capture coarse dependence, but the paper does not show that it preserves time-aligned or lagged interactions under asynchronous sampling.

The missingness evidence is narrow. The main study is confined to SolarWind, training-mask ratios are compared directly on reported test conditions, and EPA results omit BiTGraph because it failed to converge. At some EPA missingness levels Hi-Patch has better CMSE, contradicting the broad claim of consistent superiority.

Reported improvements are often small and sometimes within a weak-comparison regime. The ablation for patch masking is negligible at several missing ratios, and fixed patch sizes equal or outperform FFT patching on some datasets. No statistical tests or matched-capacity controls establish that gains arise from the claimed components rather than tuning, parameterization, or preprocessing.

Reproducibility is currently insufficient. Code is promised only after publication; dataset sizes, splits, normalization, exact channel selections, downsampling filters, software versions, fallback rules, and full baseline tuning budgets are missing. The paper also inconsistently states five random seeds in Appendix E but three in the reproducibility statement, and the confidential CHS dataset cannot independently validate the claims.

The architectural novelty is limited: the method largely combines existing channel-summary tokens, structured/read-only attention, FFT-guided patching, and PatchDropout. Given the technical issues and evaluation confounds, the evidence does not support the paper's broad 'robust real-world' framing at a top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical combination of multivariate forecasting challenges—heterogeneous sampling rates, missing input blocks, and cross-channel dependencies—that is often studied only piecemeal.

ChannelTokenFormer is a coherent architecture: per-channel patching accommodates unequal sequence lengths, channel tokens provide compact global representations, and the attention mask cleanly separates local temporal modeling from cross-channel communication.

The empirical study is broad, covering modified public benchmarks, EPA air-quality data, an industrial LNG dataset, numerous forecasting baselines, multiple horizons, and conventional as well as proposed practical settings.

Results are generally favorable and include five-seed error bars in the detailed tables. The paper also provides useful ablations of channel dependence, dynamic patching, patch masking, channel embeddings, token count, and attention-mask variants.

The scalability measurements and comparisons with an interpolation-free modified TimeXer help address efficiency and isolate some architectural benefits beyond comparisons against interpolation-based baselines.
The manuscript is clearly motivated and generally well organized, with extensive appendices and an explicit discussion of limitations and ethics.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is moderate: channel summary tokens, FFT-guided patching, patch dropout, and structured attention masks are largely adaptations or combinations of established techniques. The paper's main novelty is their integration for the proposed setting rather than a fundamentally new modeling principle.

The claimed real-world asynchrony is narrower than the framing suggests. The formulation assumes fixed, integer-related sampling periods, and most benchmarks are created by regularly downsampling synchronized datasets. This does not cover timestamp offsets, changing sampling rates, non-integer ratios, or genuinely irregular observations.

The principal SolarWind missingness experiment is unusually favorable to the method: missing blocks span exactly one patch and CTF is explicitly trained with random patch masking. It is unclear whether competing missing-aware models receive equally tuned missing-block augmentation. Missingness with arbitrary block boundaries, channel-dependent mechanisms, and distribution shift between training and testing is not adequately evaluated.

The evidence for missingness robustness beyond SolarWind is incomplete. The ETT experiment excludes dedicated missing-data methods, while the EPA experiment compares only two irregular baselines, omits BiTGraph after convergence failure, and does not consistently favor CTF at every missing ratio. The private CHS dataset is not evaluated under missingness.

The dynamic-patching specification is technically unclear. Selecting the maximum spectral amplitude and then checking whether it exceeds the spectrum's 70th percentile appears nearly tautological, and dividing an FFT-derived period in channel sample units by the relative sampling factor may double-count sampling resolution. The fallback rule is not defined precisely enough to reproduce.

Some ancillary spectral claims are overstated or questionable. Standard linear interpolation has a sinc-squared magnitude response, but the asserted frequency-dependent phase delay and creation of out-of-band energy are not generally justified as written. The measured spectral improvements over TimeXer are also very small, and architectural differences prevent attributing the entire gap solely to interpolation.

Comparison fairness is weakened by reimplementations, especially the approximation of ContiFormer's ODE solver, and by dataset-specific learning rates and other tuning choices without a clearly matched tuning budget. Statistical significance tests are not provided.

Reproducibility is currently limited because code is promised only after publication and the private industrial dataset cannot be released. There are also internal reporting inconsistencies: the appendix says error bars use five random seeds, whereas the reproducibility statement says experiments were repeated over three seeds.
